title: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Size limits of surface-tension control”. Scope: organisms and cells across sizes

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The scaling premise yields quantitative dimensionless comparisons and broad counterexample tests. Public morphology is abundant, but matched physical parameters are incomplete, so dominance can be established only for selected systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across orders of magnitude in size, calculate surface-to-volume scaling and fit shape responses to interfacial-tension versus gravity, elasticity, and active-stress models. Support requires tension-dominated predictions at cellular or minute scales and systematic loss of predictive power for large-organism form.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shape datasets rarely include all relevant forces.

Taxonomic and scale effects are confounded.

The transition size depends on material properties and environment.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public records span bacteria, small algae and large animals, so a size-stratified fit to surface-tension forms is possible after harmonising outlines. The archives were not built for that fit, and other size-linked structures predict a similar cutoff. The result would be informative for a subset of taxa and still confounded as a demonstration that molecular surface forces are the cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across a size series, measure how well outlines of whole organisms and of their cells match surface-tension surfaces, and test for a cutoff above which whole-body form departs from those surfaces while cell form still matches. That size split would support the claim; an equally good surface-tension fit for large body plans, or a poor fit already at bacterial and cellular scales, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The three archives do not share a common morphometric protocol.

Shape class is not a fit residual to a surface-tension surface.

Walls and skeletons change with size along with the surface-to-volume ratio.
